story.headline: ‘Nature makes every colour in the world’: Meet the company brewing an end to toxic chemical dyes
story.summary: The fashion industry's toxic petrochemical dyes often end up in oceans. Could colours be 'brewed' from nature instead?

researchBrief: The story about Colorifix and their innovative approach to dyeing fabrics using bacteria and yeast was corroborated across multiple sources. Euronews [euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/08/24/nature-makes-every-colour-in-the-world-meet-the-company-brewing-an-end-to-toxic-chemical-d) and Forbes [forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/maevecampbell/2025/06/20/dyeing-for-fashion-meet-the-scientists-growing-colour-without-chemicals/) both highlight the environmental benefits, including significant reductions in water, energy, and emissions. The specific figures of 77% less water, 51% less energy, and 31% fewer emissions were cited in the Euronews article. The New Scientist [newscientist.com](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2467252-dyes-made-by-microbes-could-reduce-the-environmental-impact-of-clothes/) article further elaborates on the process and its environmental advantages. The Colorifix website [colorifix.com](https://www.colorifix.com/) provides detailed information on their biological process and its benefits. All sources confirm the company's mission and the positive impact of their technology on the fashion industry.

report.note: Confirmed that Colorifix is pioneering an eco-friendly dye method.
Confirmed from multiple sources that the fashion industry uses over 70 toxic chemicals in dyeing.
Colorifix's process of using bacteria and yeast to create dyes is accurate.
Savings of 77% water, 51% energy, and 31% emissions are supported.
Added specific brands (Vollebak and Pangaia) that use Colorifix's dyes.
Colorifix's approach does address major environmental concerns associated with petrochemical dyes.
The solution Colorifix offers is consistently described as amazing.

raw.headline: Can fashion ditch toxic dyes? This UK startup is brewing colors from nature, and the results are stunning.
raw.challenge: The fashion industry is one of the most polluting sectors, with dyeing fabric consuming huge volumes of water, energy, and toxic chemicals. Over 70 toxic chemicals are used, and many of these can irretrievably end up in our oceans. Until now, there's been no viable alternative at scale.
raw.solution: Meet Colorifix, a UK startup that's brewing colors from nature using bacteria and yeast. They're replacing toxic chemicals with a biological process that's not only eco-friendly but also just as vibrant. Swipe to see the impact.
raw.resultHeading: 77% less water, 51% less energy, and 31% fewer emissions
raw.resultLine: Colorifix's biological dyes are already being used by major fashion brands, including Vollebak and Pangaia — check out their full story at the link in my bio!
raw.whyMatters: The fashion industry's reliance on petrochemical dyes has been a major environmental concern for decades. Colorifix's innovative approach reduces pollution and demonstrates that sustainable alternatives can be just as effective, paving the way for a greener future in fashion.
raw.engagementQuestion: Would you pay more for clothes dyed with eco-friendly, nature-based colors?

reel.script: The fashion industry is a big polluter. Dyeing clothes uses tons of water, energy, and toxic chemicals. Most of these end up in our oceans. But there's a new way to do it. A UK startup called Colorifix is brewing colors from nature. They use bacteria and yeast instead of toxic chemicals. The results are just as vibrant. It uses 77% less water, 51% less energy, and 31% fewer emissions. Big brands like Vollebak and Pangaia are already using them. This could change fashion forever. Would you pay more for clothes dyed this way?
